questions.question: A round apple pie is cut into 8 equal slices. 3 of the slices have whipped cream on them. What fraction of the pie has whipped cream?
questions.explain: The denominator is the number of equal parts in the whole pie (8) and the numerator is how many of those parts are shaded, so it is 3/8. A common trap is comparing the 3 creamy slices with the 5 plain ones and writing 3/5 — the bottom number must always be the whole, not the leftover part.

questions.question: A pumpkin pie is cut into 6 equal pieces. At dinner 2 pieces are eaten. What fraction of the pie is still left?
questions.explain: 6 equal pieces means the denominator is 6; 6 - 2 = 4 pieces are left, so 4/6 of the pie is left. The trap is writing 4/2, comparing the pieces left with the pieces eaten instead of with the whole pie.

questions.question: A tray holds 10 mini blueberry pies. They are packed into 5 equal boxes, with the same number of pies in each box. Sofia's family buys 2 of the boxes. What fraction of the pies did they buy?
questions.explain: Here the whole is split into 5 equal boxes, so the denominator is 5 and 2 boxes bought gives 2/5. The trap is writing 2/10, counting boxes on top but single pies on the bottom — the top and bottom must count the same kind of equal group.

questions.question: A saskatoon-berry pie is cut into 10 equal slices. Liam eats 1 slice and his sister eats 2 slices. What fraction of the pie did the two of them eat altogether?
questions.explain: They ate 1 + 2 = 3 of the 10 equal slices, so the fraction is 3/10. The trap is 3/7, comparing what was eaten with the 7 slices still on the plate — the denominator stays 10 because the whole pie is still 10 equal slices.

questions.question: On a number line from 0 to 1, the space is divided into 8 equal steps. A dot sits on the 5th mark after 0. Which fraction does the dot show?
questions.explain: On a number line the denominator is the number of equal steps between 0 and 1 (8) and the numerator is how many steps you travelled (5), giving 5/8. The trap is 5/3, comparing the steps taken with the 3 steps still to go instead of with the whole trip from 0 to 1.

questions.question: Sofia has a ribbon exactly 1 metre long. She marks it into 5 equal parts and cuts off 2 of those parts for a craft. What fraction of a metre did she cut off?
options: 2/3 of a metre
2/5 of a metre
2/100 of a metre
5/2 of a metre
questions.explain: With a length model the whole metre is the denominator's job: 5 equal parts means fifths, and 2 parts cut off is 2/5 of a metre. The trap is 2/3, comparing the 2 cut parts with the 3 parts left over rather than with all 5 equal parts.

questions.question: Zara draws a number line from 0 to 1 and splits it into 4 equal parts. Which description tells exactly where 3/4 belongs?
options: At the 3 on a line that runs from 0 to 4
Between the 3 mark and the 4 mark, because the fraction uses a 3 and a 4
3 quarter-steps from 0, three quarters of the way from 0 to 1
1 quarter-step from 0, because 1 part is left after 3 parts
questions.explain: The denominator 4 tells you to cut 0 to 1 into 4 equal steps, and the numerator 3 tells you to count 3 of those steps from 0. The trap is the one that counts the 1 leftover part instead of the 3 parts you actually travelled.

questions.question: A pack of 12 juice boxes is arranged in 3 equal rows for the soccer team. Ravi takes 1 whole row. Which statement matches what Ravi took?
options: 3/12, which is 3 juice boxes
1/12, which is 1 juice box
1/4, which is 3 juice boxes
1/3, which is 4 juice boxes
questions.explain: The pack is shared into 3 equal rows, so each row is 1/3, and 12 ÷ 3 = 4 juice boxes. The trap is 1/12, using rows on top but single juice boxes on the bottom — pick one kind of equal group and use it in both places.

questions.question: Noah has 6 hockey cards on his desk and 2 of them are goalie cards. He says the goalie cards are 2/4 of his cards, because 4 of the cards are not goalies. Which choice fixes his thinking?
options: 2/6 — the whole set is all 6 cards, so the goalie cards are 2 of 6
6/2 — the total number of cards always goes on top
2/4 — Noah is right, he compared the 2 goalie cards with the 4 other cards
4/6 — the fraction should describe the cards that are not goalies
questions.explain: In a set model the denominator must be the whole set, which is all 6 cards, so the goalie cards are 2/6. Noah made the classic mistake of comparing the part he wants with the rest of the set instead of with the whole set.

questions.question: A 1-metre measuring tape on the classroom wall is divided into 10 equal parts. Jayden's bean plant reaches the 4th mark from the bottom. Which choice gives his plant's height as a fraction of a metre and in centimetres?
options: 4/10 of a metre, which is 4 cm
4/10 of a metre, which is 40 cm
1/4 of a metre, which is 25 cm
4/6 of a metre, which is 40 cm
questions.explain: 10 equal parts in 1 metre makes each part 1/10 of a metre, so 4 parts is 4/10 of a metre, and since 1 metre is 100 cm each part is 10 cm, giving 40 cm. Two traps hide here: comparing the 4 parts with the 6 parts above the plant, and forgetting to change metres into centimetres.

questions.question: Ella and Ben each bring an identical banana loaf to the bake sale, and each loaf is cut into 8 equal slices. Ella sells 5 of her slices and Ben sells 3 of his. What fraction of the two loaves did they sell altogether?
options: 8/8 of the two loaves
5/8 of the two loaves
8/16 of the two loaves
16/8 of the two loaves
questions.explain: When the whole is both loaves, the denominator counts every equal slice: 8 + 8 = 16, and they sold 5 + 3 = 8 slices, so 8/16 (which is one half). The trap is 8/8, keeping the denominator of a single loaf even though the question asks about two loaves — always check what the whole is first.

questions.question: A class of 24 students is split into 4 equal relay teams. Two of the teams wear red pinnies. Tyler says 2/24 of the class wears red. Which statement is correct?
options: 2/24 of the class, which is 2 students
4/2 of the class, which is more than the whole class
2/2 of the class, because 2 teams wear red and 2 teams do not
2/4 of the class, which is 12 students
questions.explain: The class is shared into 4 equal teams, so the denominator is 4, and 2 teams in red is 2/4 of the class; since 24 ÷ 4 = 6 students per team, that is 12 students. Tyler's mistake was counting teams on top and single students on the bottom — both numbers must count the same kind of equal group.
